What size power station do you need to keep a Starlink Mini running?

Scenarios Updated 2026-08-08

Almost any power station clears the wattage: Starlink Mini draws at most 40 W while running, well under what a coffee maker or a hair dryer asks for. The question that actually decides which machine you need is watt-hours per day, because the dish has no real idle mode and is designed to stay connected continuously.

Size on the top of the published band: 40 W — the one end both Starlink documents agree on — held for a full day works out to 960 Wh. That multiplication is ours, not Starlink’s: the company publishes a draw, never a daily total. It is more than a small power station holds and comfortably inside a mid-size one.

Official spec · verified 2026-08-01 · Starlink Mini record

Look at the last two rows together and the dish stops looking like a normal idle-capable appliance. Idle draw is 15 W, three-quarters of the low end of the running figure above it. Most electronics drop to a small fraction of their running draw when nothing is happening; this one barely drops at all, because a phased-array antenna and its routing electronics stay active whether or not anything is streaming through them. The only real saving is switching it off — there is no low-power state worth waiting for.

What a full day of uptime costs

Daily energy, continuous operation

Starlink publishes a draw in watts and nothing per day, so both figures here are ours: a published running figure multiplied by twenty-four hours, with the multiplication stated on each row. They are shown as the two ends of the band rather than as one number, for the same reason the card above shows a disagreement rather than an average.

Per day, at the bottom of the band 480 Wh Derived by WattPair

The support article’s 20 W floor times twenty-four hours. Starlink’s specification sheet puts that floor at 25 W instead — a documented disagreement between two of the company’s own current documents — which would make this row nearer 600 Wh. Neither candidate is averaged away.

Per day, at the top of the band — the figure to size on 960 Wh Derived by WattPair

40 W, the end of the running band both Starlink documents agree on, times twenty-four hours. This is the sizing floor carried on the load record, and it is this site’s arithmetic rather than a published Starlink figure. Inverter losses are not in it.

Derived by WattPair · verified 2026-08-01 · Starlink Mini record

What that is on three real machines

Left running continuously, BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 covers 6.3 h — under a third of a day. BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 reaches 21 h, roughly 0.9 days. BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 covers 40 h, or about 1.7 days — the first of the three that gets you through an unattended trip without a recharge.

This is a battery question, not a wattage question

Every machine in our library clears the running watts above with room to spare; none of the three pairings here is decided by whether the station can switch the dish on. The only thing that moves between them is how many hours of a continuous, unchanging load the battery holds — exactly the arithmetic the runtime calculator performs. Those hour figures are the engine running the load record’s headline draw, which sits in the middle of the published band; at the top of the band each one is roughly a quarter shorter.

Why the sizing guidance is bigger than the running draw

Our own sizing guidance for this dish asks for a continuous rating of 60 W, roughly double the running figure above. Starlink does not ask for that — we do. It is not a measured start-up spike either, because Starlink publishes no inrush current for this product: 60 W is the rated ceiling of the power supply the kit ships with, which we adopt as a conservative stand-in for a number nobody published. Treat it as headroom rather than as evidence of a surge event — nothing in the manufacturer’s documentation describes one.

The USB-C port is not a safe assumption

Starlink states that powering the Mini over USB-C needs a supply capable of 100 W at 20 V and 5 A, with its own adapter cable — well above what most power stations’ USB-C ports deliver. The manufacturer guarantees performance only with the included power supply and cable; the safer route on a power station is its DC or car-style output rather than USB-C.

Questions people ask

What size power station do I need for a Starlink Mini?
Size on watt-hours per day, not on wattage. The dish draws 20–40 W running and 15 W idle, which almost any power station can switch on; the number that separates machines is whether the battery holds close to a kilowatt-hour. That target is our arithmetic rather than a Starlink figure: 40 W, the top of the published band and the one end both Starlink documents agree on, held for twenty-four hours is 960 Wh. Starlink publishes a draw, not a daily total.
Does turning a Starlink Mini off between uses save much power?
More than you would expect from most electronics, because this one has no efficient low-power idle state. Idle draw sits at three-quarters of the low end of its running draw, so leaving it connected around the clock costs nearly as much as leaving it in active use.
Can I power a Starlink Mini from a power station’s USB-C port?
Only if that port can deliver the 100 W at 20 V/5 A Starlink specifies for USB-C power, with its own cable — most power station USB-C outputs fall short of that. The manufacturer’s guaranteed path is the included power supply, or a power station’s DC/car-style output at the dish’s native 12–48 V input.
